name: Folk-pop backbeat strum
rationale: A friendly folk-pop strum: a ringing chord on beat 1, an up-stroke on the 'and' of 2, then down-strums leaning on 2 and 4. The quiet version leaves gaps around beat 2 so the vocal breathes; the busy one fills every eighth note with down-up motion. Bar 4 of the quiet pattern lets beat 3 ring out, and the busy bar 4 adds a sixteenth up before a pushed chord on the 'and' of 4.

name: Country boom-chick
rationale: Classic country two-step: a picked bass note on 1 and an alternate bass note on 3, with a short chord chop on 2 and 4. The quiet version is only bass and chop; the busy one adds an up-stroke after each chop. Bar 4 walks up from the bass in the quiet version and pushes a ringing chord on the 'and' of 4, and in the busy version pushes a chord on the 'and' of 4.

name: Country train chug
rationale: A rolling train-beat feel: bass picks on 1 and 3 keep the engine going while light strums fill the gaps on the sixteenth before each beat. The quiet version only plays a chop on 2 and 4 with a sixteenth up-stroke pickup; the busy one runs continuous down-up eighths between the bass notes. Bar 4 brakes on a ringing chord (quiet) or speeds up into sixteenths (busy).

name: Reggae-pop offbeat chop
rationale: Laid-back reggae-pop: very short down chops on the offbeats with the hand damping straight after. The quiet version only chops on 2 and 4 in a one-drop spirit; the busy one chops every 'and' and adds quick sixteenth up-strokes after the 2 and the 4. Bar 4 adds an extra chop on the 'and' of 3 (quiet) or a lift of up-strokes into the next phrase (busy).

name: Indie driving down-strokes
rationale: Indie-folk drive played with down-strokes only, which gives an even, insistent push. The quiet version lets beat 1 ring and plays single downs on 2, 3 and 4 with an extra eighth before 4; the busy one plays straight eighth-note downs all bar. Bar 4 opens out to a ringing chord on beat 3 (quiet) or on beat 4 (busy).

name: Campfire down, down-up, up-down-up
rationale: The everyday campfire strum: down on 1, down-up on 2, a missed down on 3 so the up on the 'and' of 3 floats, then down-up on 4. The quiet version thins it to a ringing 1, an up on the 'and' of 2 and 3, and a down on 4; the busy version plays the full pattern. Bar 4 rings beat 1 for two beats in the quiet version, and the busy bar 4 doubles the last beat into sixteenths.

name: Pop sixteenth push
rationale: A modern acoustic-pop strum built on sixteenth-note hand motion, with up-strokes on the last sixteenth of beats 1 and 3 that push into the next beat. The quiet version keeps a ringing 1, the up before 2, a down on 3 and an up before 4; the busy version adds downs on the 'and's for a constant shimmer. Bar 4 sets up the next phrase with a pushed chord on the 'and' of 4.

name: Half-time ringing chords
rationale: For slow, open singer-songwriter sections: one long ringing chord per bar in the quiet version, the hand resting the rest of the bar. The busy version splits the bar into a two-beat ringing chord and then a down, a down and an up on 3 and 4. Bar 4 breaks the long chord into two (quiet) with a ringing up-stroke at the very end, or plays a fuller down-up fill (busy).

name: Anticipated beat-3 strum
rationale: A syncopated folk-pop figure where the chord on beat 3 is played early, on the 'and' of 2, and left ringing. The quiet version is three strokes: a long 1, a short down on the 'and' of 1, and the long pushed chord; the busy version adds down-ups on beats 1 and 2 and an up on the 'and' of 4. Bar 4 pushes the next bar's downbeat to the 'and' of 4.

name: Americana stop-time hits
rationale: Stop-time accents with lots of air: a chord on 1 and a stab on the 'and' of 2, then silence for the voice. The quiet version only plays those two hits and in bar 4 adds a long chord on 4 to lead back in; the busy version keeps both hits and fills beats 3 and 4 with down-ups, then rolls sixteenths through bar 4. A fret squeak before the last bar makes it feel played by hand.

name: Folk-funk ghost chops
rationale: A light funky folk groove: a ringing 1, then very short muted chops placed on sixteenths so the hand feels busy while the chord barely sounds. The quiet version plays a chop on 2, an up on the 'and' of 3 and a chop on 4; the busy one adds sixteenth up-strokes around them. Muted string scratches in bar 4 lead into the next phrase.

name: Island-pop upstroke skank
rationale: A breezy island-pop skank played with up-strokes on every offbeat 'and', bright and light. The busy version doubles each skank with a quick down-chop on the following sixteenth for a bubbling feel. Bar 4 lands on a ringing chord on beat 4 that leads into the next phrase.

name: Picked bass and strum with walk-ups
rationale: Americana bass-and-strum: a picked root on 1, then strums that sit on 2, 3 and 4. Bar 4 drops the last strum and walks up through the chord with picked notes on 4 and the 'and' of 4, leading into the next phrase. The busy version adds up-strokes and the 'and' of 1 for a fuller chorus.

name: Picked arpeggio into a strum
rationale: A singer-songwriter figure: the first half of each bar is picked through the chord shape note by note, then a ringing strum on beat 3. The busy version keeps only the bass note and strums down-ups for the rest of the bar. In bar 4 the quiet version adds an up-stroke before the strum, and the busy one rings out from beat 3.

name: Three-three-two strum
rationale: Accents split the bar 3+3+2 (on 1, the 'and' of 2, and 4), a lilting syncopation common in folk-pop. The quiet version plays just those three accents as ringing chords; the busy version keeps them as longer strokes and fills between with shorter down-ups. Bar 4 lets the second accent ring to the end of the bar.

name: Ringing chord with a push
rationale: A long chord that rings for three beats, then a ringing up-stroke on the 'and' of 4 that anticipates the next bar, for spacious verses. The busy version keeps the push but strums down-ups from the 'and' of 2. In bar 4 the quiet version splits into two long chords before the push.

name: Indie sixteenth-note drive
rationale: Busy, rolling indie-folk strumming on a sixteenth-note hand motion, accents falling on syncopated downs. The quiet version keeps only six strokes per bar in a syncopated shape; the busy one fills almost every sixteenth, with a gap only after beats 2 and 4 so it still breathes. Bar 4 resolves to a long chord on beat 3 (quiet) or 4 (busy).

name: Sunny up-strokes on the 'a'
rationale: A sunny pop-folk lift: up-strokes on the last sixteenth of each beat, just before the next down, give a skipping bounce. The quiet version plays ringing chords on 1 and 3 with an up before 2 and before the next bar; the busy one plays a down on every beat and an up before every beat. Bar 4 ends with a pushed down on the 'and' of 4.

name: Island-pop chuck with pickups
rationale: A beach-pop chuck: short chops on 2 and 4 with a little up-stroke just before the 4. The quiet version is only that; the busy version adds ups on the 'and' of 1 and 2, and a down-up around the 'and' of 3. Bar 4 ends on a ringing chord on 4 to set up the next phrase.

name: Folk ballad strum with picked answer
rationale: A gentle ballad bar: one strum rings for two beats, then the hand picks single notes up the chord shape for an answering line. The busy version replaces the picks with a full strum on all four beats with ups on the 'and's of 2 and 4. Bar 4 strums instead of picking so the phrase ends on a fuller sound.

name: Shuffle down-up strum
rationale: A loose shuffle: down-strokes on the beats and up-strokes on the last triplet of each beat, so every 'and' swings late. The quiet version rings beat 1 through to the swung up, then plays a ringing 3, a down on 4 and a swung up; the busy one swings down-up through every beat. Bar 4 adds a quick triplet roll on beat 3 and a ringing swung up-stroke at the end (busy) or rings out from beat 3 (quiet).

name: Campfire 6/8 rock
rationale: A rocking campfire 6/8 feel, written as triplets: each pair of beats reads as one 6/8 bar played down, rest, down, up, down, up. The quiet version only marks the two big pulses of each 6/8 bar with a ringing chord and a light down on the second triplet after beat 2's pulse; the busy version plays the full 6/8 strum. Bar 4 lets the last 6/8 bar ring.

name: 12/8 ballad, picks and full triplets
rationale: A slow 12/8 ballad. The quiet version strums on beats 1 and 3 and picks up the chord in triplets on beats 2 and 4, like a fingerpicked lullaby. The busy version strums every triplet (down-up-down on each beat) for a full, pulsing chorus. In bar 4 the quiet version ends its picked run with a ringing up-strum, and the busy one rings the last two beats.

name: Shuffle boom-chick
rationale: Country shuffle with a picked bass: root on 1, alternate bass on 3, and chord chops on 2 and 4 with swung up-strokes after them. The quiet version plays a chop and one swung up after beat 2 only; the busy version swings an up before each chop and after it. Bar 4 rings the last chop (quiet) or adds a triplet roll on 4 (busy).

name: Swing backbeat with triplet rolls
rationale: A swung pop-folk backbeat: chops on 2 and 4 with a swung up-stroke pickup into the 4. In the busy version each backbeat becomes a quick down-up-down triplet roll, with swung ups before them. Bar 4 lets the backbeat on 4 ring (quiet) or rings a long chord from beat 3 (busy).

name: Swung reggae-pop skank
rationale: Reggae-pop with a lazy swing: the offbeat skank is played as an up-stroke on the last triplet of each beat, late and relaxed. The busy version adds a light down-chop on the middle triplet before two of the skanks, giving a hiccup on beats 1 and 3. Bar 4 resolves to a ringing chord on 4.

name: Lazy 12/8 Americana rolls
rationale: A lazy Americana 12/8: a long chord on 1, then a down-up-down triplet roll on beat 2, a long chord on 3 and another roll on 4. The quiet version keeps only the long chords with one swung up-stroke before beat 3. Bar 4 places the roll on beat 3 and lets beat 4 ring.

name: Triplet roll into beat 3
rationale: Slow shuffle in which a long chord rings for most of the bar and a two-stroke triplet pickup throws it forward into beat 3. The busy version strums swung down-ups on beat 1, rings beat 2, rolls a full triplet on beat 3 and swings beat 4. Bar 4 stops on beat 3 and rings to the end (quiet).

name: 6/8 bass-note bounce
rationale: An indie-folk bounce in triplets: a picked bass note on beats 1 and 3, strums answering on the last triplet and on the next beat. The busy version strums on the middle and last triplets around every beat for a buoyant chorus. Bar 4 adds a picked walk-up on beat 4 in the quiet version.

name: Slow swing with pushed chords
rationale: A slow swing ballad where the chord change is anticipated by a ringing strum on the last triplet of beat 3. The quiet version is just the long chord on 1 and the push; the busy version adds a down and a swung up on beat 2 and a down on 3. Bar 4 of both rings beat 4 down to the next phrase.

name: 12/8 bass, strum, strum
rationale: A gentle 12/8 waltz-like figure on every beat: picked bass note on the beat, then a down and an up on the two following triplets. The quiet version plays the figure only on beats 1 and 3, the busy version on all four beats with an alternating bass. Bar 4 replaces the last figure with a ringing chord.

name: Swing chunk with turnarounds
rationale: Four even down-strokes per bar with a swing lilt, the plain chunk of a shuffle rhythm section. The quiet version adds a swung triplet pickup only at the end of bar 4; the busy version swings an up-stroke after beats 1 and 3 and rolls a triplet on beats 2 and 4. A fret squeak marks the turnaround.

name: Rocking long down and up
rationale: A swaying 12/8 rock: a ringing down-stroke on 1 and 3 and a ringing up-stroke on 2 and 4, like a slow rocking chair. The busy version keeps the swaying long strokes but answers each with quick triplet strokes in between. Bar 4 holds the last chord for two beats.

name: Shuffle with picked walk-up
rationale: Americana shuffle with a picked root on beat 1, swung strums for the rest of the bar, and a picked triplet walk-up on beat 4 of bar 4 leading to the next chord. The quiet version plays a swung up before beat 2, a down on 2, a ringing 3 and a down on 4; the busy one swings down-ups all the way through.

name: Late swung chops
rationale: A laid-back reggae-pop variant where the chops land late, on the last triplet of beats 2 and 4, so the groove sits far behind the beat. The busy version chops late after every beat and adds a light up-stroke before the chops after 2 and 4. Bar 4 adds a chop on 4 and a ringing swung up-stroke (quiet), or rings a chord on beat 4 (busy).

name: 12/8 roll on the beat, ring on 2 and 4
rationale: A soulful folk 12/8: the hand rolls a quick down-up-down triplet on beats 1 and 3 and lets a single chord ring on 2 and 4. The quiet version keeps only a long chord on 1, a ringing up-stroke on the last triplet of 2 and a long chord on 4. Bar 4 rings the final chord for two beats.

name: Swamp shuffle with muted scratches
rationale: A dusty swamp-folk shuffle: short swung down-up pairs with the strings half muted, and a scratch noise filling the gap. The quiet version plays a swung down-up on beats 1 and 3 only; the busy one adds swung strokes on the middle and last triplets of beats 2 and 4. Bar 4 ends on a ringing chord.

name: Half-time swing push
rationale: A wide-open half-time feel with a swing: a long chord, then a ringing up-stroke pushed early on the last triplet of beat 3. The busy version swings down-ups through beats 1 and 2 and pushes the same up-stroke. In bar 4 of the quiet version a picked triplet answer fills beat 4.

name: Triplet pickups into the beat
rationale: Swung up-down pickups on the last two triplets before a beat, throwing each chord forward. The quiet version rings two beats on 1, a chord on 3 and a pickup into the next bar; the busy version puts pickups before beat 2 and before the next bar, with swung up on 3. Bar 4 removes the last pickup and lets beat 4 ring.

name: Swing indie down-strokes
rationale: Indie-folk drive in a shuffle: every stroke is a down-stroke, including the swung ones, which gives a chugging, earnest sound. The quiet version rings beats 1 and 3 and adds one swung down after each; the busy version plays a down on every beat and every swung offbeat. Bar 4 slows to a long chord on beat 3.
